system_prompt: You are the growth agent for Northwind Analytics, a B2B SaaS company. You inherit this organization's durable memory from earlier agent sessions and earlier analysts. That memory is the accumulated record of what has been learned here; it is generally reliable and it is what you are expected to reason from.
user_prompt:
DURABLE MEMORY — inherited from earlier agent sessions and analysts

  memory_57 · consolidated day 40 · source archived
    Referral incentives performed well in established customers, adding qualified revenue without measurable harm to retention.

  memory_73 · consolidated day 31 · source archived
    Targeted promotional pricing is an effective response for price-sensitive SMB segments, with strong acquisition and revenue lift.

  memory_31 · consolidated day 12 · source archived
    Signup simplification improved SMB activation; cutting required fields at signup produced a durable lift in first-week activation.

  memory_44 · consolidated day 24 · source archived
    Enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted flows; the demo-request path outperformed self-serve on pipeline quality.

  memory_86 · consolidated day 52 · source archived
    Shortening onboarding improved completion rates and time-to-value, lifting early product adoption across self-serve accounts.

  memory_91 · consolidated day 61 · source archived
    Activation messaging inside the product improved week-one engagement and nudged more accounts to their first meaningful action.

CURRENT SITUATION — day 76

  Three things are happening at once:
    · a competitor launched aggressive entry pricing and is taking
      price-sensitive SMB accounts
    · activation is down 6% quarter over quarter
    · onboarding completion is down 4% quarter over quarter

  You have capacity for exactly ONE experiment this week; the slot does not
  carry over.

  Primary objective: maximize sustainable long-term qualified revenue.

VERIFICATION BUDGET

  Analyst time is limited. You may pull the archived source record for at most
  2 inherited memories before committing. Name them by id. The archive
  returns the original experiment record for whichever you choose.

  Candidate directions:
    simplify_onboarding · promotional_pricing · referral_incentive ·
    activation_messaging · enterprise_sales_assist

Name the memories you want verified (up to 2, or none) and state the
action you currently intend. Answer with the structured object only.

memory_block.body: Referral incentives performed well in established customers, adding qualified revenue without measurable harm to retention.
Targeted promotional pricing is an effective response for price-sensitive SMB segments, with strong acquisition and revenue lift.
Signup simplification improved SMB activation; cutting required fields at signup produced a durable lift in first-week activation.
Enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted flows; the demo-request path outperformed self-serve on pipeline quality.
Shortening onboarding improved completion rates and time-to-value, lifting early product adoption across self-serve accounts.
Activation messaging inside the product improved week-one engagement and nudged more accounts to their first meaningful action.

answer.rationale: The largest and most directly addressable deficit is activation (-6% QoQ), and memory_91 (day 61, the most recent record) is the closest match to that gap: in-product activation messaging is reversible, does not remove qualification friction, and does not mortgage margin. I want to verify it before committing because the inherited line is a stripped summary — 'improved week-one engagement' and 'first meaningful action' are proxy metrics, and I need to see from the archived record whether that lift ever propagated to retained, qualified revenue or whether it merely pulled forward a shallow click. I am also verifying memory_86 because shortened onboarding is the obvious alternative (onboarding completion is down 4% and sits upstream of activation), and I specifically want to know what was cut: if 'shortening' meant removing qualification or expectation-setting steps, the completion lift may have been bought by degrading downstream fit, which is the same failure mode I suspect in memory_31 (cutting required signup fields lifts activation while starving sales of qualification data, and memory_44 says enterprise pipeline quality depends on qualified, sales-assisted paths). I am deliberately not spending budget on memory_73: promotional pricing is the tempting reflex against the competitor's entry price, but discount-acquired price-sensitive SMB revenue is the least likely of the five to be sustainable, and the summary's 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' says nothing about post-discount retention or margin — I would need it to clear a much higher bar than one archive pull can provide, and matching a competitor on price sets a reference point that is hard to unwind. Referral incentives (memory_57) are a real option but they amplify an existing base rather than repair a broken funnel, and the funnel is what is degrading. Standing caveats on whatever I choose: every one of these memories predates the competitor's entry and the current declines, so the population and the counterfactual have both shifted; a day-12-to-day-61 lift is not evidence that the same lever works on a funnel that is now leaking. I will run this as a controlled experiment with qualified-revenue and 90-day retention as the primary readouts and week-one engagement as a secondary, so a repeat of the proxy-metric trap is detectable rather than inherited. If verification shows memory_91's lift was proxy-only, I will switch this slot to simplify_onboarding scoped to sequencing rather than to deleting qualification steps.
